William Jennings Bryan. At the 1896 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, this relatively unknown delegate delivered an electrifying address that catapulted him to the presidential nomination and became the defining statement of American Populism.

The speech's central image was unforgettable: "You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold." Bryan yoked monetary policy to Christian martyrdom, attacking the gold standard as a tool of the wealthy. He argued that free coinage of silver would help farmers and workers, rejecting the notion that wage workers were merely the businessmen's equals. Instead, he asserted the dignity of labor itself.

The convention erupted. Bryan won the nomination on the first ballot. Though he lost the presidential election to McKinley, the speech exemplified Populism's moral vocabulary. We have petitioned, he said, and our petitions have been scorned. That phrase "cross of gold" entered the language as shorthand for oppressive economic systems, and Bryan's moral vision shaped American populism for generations to come.
